title: Getting back what you thought you lost
objective: By the end of this lesson you can recover a deleted branch, an overwritten commit, or a bad reset — and you know the one case where recovery is genuinely impossible.

blocks.text: Almost every Git horror story ends the same way: the work was still there. Git keeps a private log of everywhere your branch pointers have been, and that log is what turns most disasters into a two-command fix.
The reflog: a record of where you have been

Every time HEAD moves — a commit, a switch, a merge, a reset, a rebase — Git appends a line to the reflog. It is local, it is private to your machine, and it holds entries for 90 days by default — but only 30 for entries pointing at commits nothing else references, which is exactly the case you reach for it in.

blocks.caption: Reading it
lines: a3f91c2 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
9d2e8b1 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add the validation step   ← the work you thought was gone
7c1a4f8 HEAD@{2}: commit: Add the upload form
5b9d3e2 HEAD@{3}: checkout: moving from main to feature/upload

blocks.text: Rescue 1: a reset that went too far

blocks.caption: Go back to where you were
lines: git reflog                     # find the entry from before the reset
git reset --hard 9d2e8b1       # return to that exact state

blocks.caption: The branch label is gone, the commits are not
lines: git reflog                          # find the last commit that was on it
git branch feature/upload 9d2e8b1   # put the label back
# Deleting a branch only removes the pointer.
# The commits stay until Git's garbage collection removes unreachable ones.

blocks.text: Rescue 3: an amend that ate the previous message or content

blocks.caption: The old commit is still recorded
lines: git reflog                    # the pre-amend commit is listed
git show HEAD@{1}             # look at it before deciding
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}     # or recover it entirely

blocks.title: Look before you leap, twice
blocks.text: git show <id> lets you inspect any commit from the reflog before you act on it. Recovering into the wrong state is its own small disaster — and since reset --hard is usually the recovery command, take the extra ten seconds to confirm you have the right entry.
The one thing that cannot be recovered

The reflog records commits. Work that was never committed — edits sitting in your working directory, or changes you staged but never committed — has no reflog entry, so no reflog command finds them. One narrow exception: changes you staged but never committed were written into the object database as blobs, and git fsck --lost-found can still recover those until gc runs. Unstaged edits leave nothing behind at all. git restore, git checkout of a file, and reset --hard all discard that work permanently.

blocks.title: Which is why commits are the real safety net
blocks.text: A commit, even a scruffy one on a throwaway branch, leaves a record you can find again — which uncommitted work never does. That record is not permanent, though: Git expires reflog entries for unreachable commits after 30 days by default (90 for reachable ones), and housekeeping then removes the commits themselves. Recovery is reliable in the days after a mistake, not months later. Uncommitted work is the only thing with no record. If you are about to do something risky, the cheapest insurance is to commit first — you can always tidy the history afterwards, and this lesson is why that is true.

rows: git reflog then reset --hard to the earlier entry
No reflog entry — but the blob is in the object database; git fsck --lost-found finds it until gc runs

blocks.title: Destroy some work, then get it back
steps: Run: echo important > important.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Add important work"
Run: git log --oneline -2      (note your commit id)
Run: git reset --hard HEAD~1   (the commit is gone from the branch)
Run: git log --oneline -2      (confirm it is not there)
Run: git reflog                (it is right there in the reflog)
Run: git reset --hard HEAD@{1} && cat important.txt
Run: git switch main && git branch -D rescue-demo && git reflog
Run: git branch rescued <the id from the reflog> && git switch rescued && ls
blocks.expected: A commit deleted and recovered, then an entire branch deleted and rebuilt from the reflog. Doing this once in a sandbox removes most of the fear that makes people avoid the useful parts of Git.

cheatsheet: git reflog — every position HEAD has held, kept locally for 90 days, or 30 when nothing else references the commit
Recover a bad reset: git reset --hard HEAD@{1} (or the id from the reflog)
Recover a deleted branch: git branch <name> <id from reflog>
Recover an amended commit: the pre-amend version is in the reflog
Recover from a rebase: the original commits are in the reflog
git show <id> — inspect before you act on it
Deleting a branch removes only the label; the commits remain reachable via reflog
Uncommitted work has no record and cannot be recovered — commit before anything risky

choices.C: Every position HEAD has pointed to

checkpoint.explanation: Commits, switches, merges, resets, rebases. It is a local log of pointer movement, which is exactly what you need to return to a state you left by accident.

checkpoint.prompt: You deleted a branch with git branch -D and it had unmerged commits. What is true?

choices.B: Only the branch label was removed
choices.D: You must restore from a backup

checkpoint.explanation: The commits are still reachable via the reflog and the branch can be recreated. A branch is a pointer. Deleting the pointer does not delete the commits — git branch <name> <id> puts the label back.

checkpoint.prompt: Which of these is genuinely unrecoverable?

choices.A: Uncommitted edits discarded with git restore
choices.B: A commit removed by reset --hard, if it was recent

checkpoint.explanation: The reflog records commits. Work that was never committed has no entry, so there is nothing to return to.

checkpoint.prompt: You are about to attempt something risky in a repository. What is the cheapest insurance?

choices.A: Push to the remote immediately, before anything goes wrong
choices.B: Commit your work first, even to a scruffy branch
choices.C: Copy the folder to your desktop

checkpoint.explanation: A recent commit is usually recoverable through a reflog while its entry still exists and before unreachable objects are garbage-collected. A temporary branch also gives the commit a reachable name, which is safer than relying on reflog expiry windows.
